hints_cache: Since $n$ is a billion but there are only a few restrictions, don't focus on every building. Focus on the restricted buildings and the empty spaces between them.

A restriction at one building affects its neighbors. If building 10 is capped at 2, building 9 can't be taller than 3, and building 11 can't be taller than 3 either. This 'pressure' spreads in both directions.

To find the 'true' height limit of a building, you must reconcile its own cap with the caps of every other restricted building. Try a two-pass approach: one pass to let constraints flow right, and another to let them flow left.
Don't forget the edges! You should treat the first building (height 0 at index 1) and the last building (index $n$) as special restrictions to ensure your logic covers the whole range.

Once you have the final height limits for all restricted points, the maximum height between two points $(d1, h1)$ and $(d2, h2)$ can be found using a simple formula involving the distance between them and their height difference.
